extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, and students preparing scholarly manuscripts (especially in the humanities and arts)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing notes and bibliographies (Chicago's notes-and-bibliography system) and for citing sources (including quotations, URLs, DOIs, and electronic resources) in scholarly works, with formatting rules and practical recommendations for authors and editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play text references format
rubrics_metrics.description: Text references are to act, scene, and line of this edition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give parenthetical references to plays as act.scene.line (example: (3.4.46-47)). When multiple sources or different editions of a single source are used, indicate the title or edition in the parenthetical references; consider devising abbreviations for each and include a list of abbreviations at the beginning or end of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement and punctuation for run-in quotation sources
rubrics_metrics.description: After a run-in quotation, the source is usually given after the closing quotation mark, followed by the rest of the surrounding sentence (including any comma, semicolon, colon, or dash) or the final punctuation of that sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show the parenthetical citation immediately after the closing quotation mark and the sentence then continuing with normal punctuation (see examples in text). A parenthetical reference need not immediately follow the quotation as long as it is clear what it belongs to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation when quotation ends with question/exclamation
rubrics_metrics.description: When a quotation comes at the end of a sentence and is itself a question or an exclamation, that punctuation is retained within the quotation marks, and a period is still added after the closing parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Lear rails, “Why should a dog…?” (5.3.306-7). Note the question mark inside the quotes and the period after the closing parenthesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parenthetical source placement for block quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: The source of a block quotation is given in parentheses at the end of the quotation and in the same type size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opening parenthesis appears after the final punctuation mark of the quoted material. No period either precedes or follows the closing parenthesis. Shortened references are treated the same as full ones; qualifiers such as line, vol., or p., when required at the beginning of a shortened reference, should be lowercased.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parenthetical citations with poetry extracts
rubrics_metrics.description: Parenthetical citations following poetry extracts are dropped to the line below the last line of the quotation so as not to interfere with a poem’s layout and presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They may be centered on the last letter of the longest line or set flush with the left margin of the poem; an additional line space may be added. Other positions are possible; the key is consistency and clarity. Shortened references to poetry are treated the same as full ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of source citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Source citations must provide sufficient information either to lead readers directly to the sources consulted or to enable readers to positively identify them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This applies regardless of whether the sources are published or unpublished or in printed or electronic form. Conventions vary by discipline, publisher, and work needs, but citations must always allow readers to judge and locate the source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice between Chicago's two systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Chicago describes two systems of source citation: the notes-and-bibliography system (uses notes and bibliography) and the author-date system (uses parenthetical author-date references and a reference list).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes-and-bibliography is preferred by many writers in literature, history, and the arts; author-date is preferred in many sciences and social sciences. For journals, follow the journal's specified system and consult its instructions to authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility vs. consistency in style
rubrics_metrics.description: Logical and defensible variations on the illustrated styles are acceptable if agreed to by author and publisher, but consistency must be maintained within a work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals often require strict adherence to an established style; for book-length works, negotiated and consistent deviations are acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of citation-management tools (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Citation management applications (e.g., EndNote, Zotero) allow users to build libraries of reference data and to place notes or generate bibliographies formatted to many citation styles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such tools make creating citations easy but results are only as good as the input data and software formatting. Authors are strongly encouraged to review generated citations for accuracy and completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-check your citation data
rubrics_metrics.description: As you build your library of source data, check each field against the actual source as soon as you acquire the data for it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify authors’ names, titles, dates, and ensure fields are entered appropriately. Check for missing or redundant data. It's acceptable to collect more data than used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-check your citations in the manuscript
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a source citation has been inserted in your manuscript, make sure it is correctly formatted according to the recommendations in this chapter or chapter 15.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for errant punctuation or capitalization and missing or superfluous data; enter corrections in the citation management application (or adjust settings) and double-check results in the manuscript. Publishers may require citations as ordinary text—check formatting after conversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Back up citation data
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure your citations are backed up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some applications back up automatically; keep local copies as a safeguard. Save a backup copy of the penultimate manuscript version with citation codes intact in case citations need regeneration.

rubrics_metrics.name: URLs as electronic resource identifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors citing sources consulted online should generally include a URL as the final element in a citation that includes the other citation components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A URL can lead readers directly to the source; include URLs when helpful, but record full facts of publication first. Consult publishers early about their URL requirements (book publishers may require URLs only when otherwise difficult to locate). See related sections for DOIs and other electronic formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for DOIs (Digital Object Identifiers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should prefer a DOI- or Handle-based URL whenever one is available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A DOI forms a persistent URL beginning with https://doi.org/ plus the prefix and suffix (e.g., https://doi.org/10.1086/679716). Append the DOI to https://doi.org/ to form a URL. DOIs are preferred because they redirect to the latest version and persist across moves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use permalinks / persistent URLs when available
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer permalinks, persistent URLs, or stable URLs provided with internet resources over volatile search-result links.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test such links to ensure they lead where intended. When a DOI or Handle exists, prefer it. If a URL points to a paywalled database, consider naming the database instead (see library/database guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid third-party shorteners for citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Shortened versions of a URL provided by third-party services (intended primarily for social media) should never be used in formal citations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such services can disappear and the original URL better identifies domain and important citation elements. Publishers may make exceptions (e.g., for DOIs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming subscription databases instead of URL
rubrics_metrics.description: For sources consulted via a library or commercial bibliographic database and available only through subscription, it may be best to name the database in lieu of a URL.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test the URL while logged out—if it leads to a login page only, naming the database is safer. Prefer DOI-based URLs when available, since they direct to source information even without subscription access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access dates for online sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Chicago does not require access dates in published citations of electronic sources unless no date of publication or revision can be determined from the source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some publishers, disciplines, or students may require access dates; authors should check publisher requirements and it is good practice to record access dates during research (citation tools can capture these automatically).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include revision/'last modified' date when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a 'last modified' or revision date if it is presented as the de facto date of publication or is otherwise the only available date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such dates may be particularly useful for citing wikis and other frequently updated works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh authority and permanence of electronic sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must weigh the authority of any electronic sources; content without formal ties to a publisher or sponsoring body has the authority equivalent to unpublished or self-published material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unpublished electronic content is more likely to change or disappear. Self-published material from an authority may be relied on, but anything posted online is 'published' for copyright and must be cited fully and considered for permissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve a permanent record of nonformal sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors are strongly encouraged to keep a copy of any source that is not formally published as a hedge against future changes or disappearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: social-media posts, bank webpages, versions of news articles. Keep printouts, PDFs, screen captures, or use permanent-link services such as Perma.cc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite the version/medium consulted
rubrics_metrics.description: When publications are available in more than one medium, authors should cite the version consulted and Chicago recommends including a URL to indicate an online consultation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternate electronic formats from the same publisher (PDF vs HTML) need not be separately indicated. A DOI-based URL technically points to all published media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation rules for URLs in text
rubrics_metrics.description: URLs should be presented in full, beginning with the protocol (http or https); the protocol letter is not capitalized. The trailing slash is part of the URL; capitalization of case-sensitive components should not be edited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid beginning a sentence with a URL. Sentences including a URL should be punctuated normally; angle brackets or wrappers are unnecessary in notes, bibliographies, or running text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breaking URLs at line ends in print
rubrics_metrics.description: If a URL must be broken at the end of a line in print, break after a colon or a double slash (//); before a single slash (/), a tilde (~), a period, a comma, a hyphen, an underline (_), a question mark, a number sign, or a percent symbol; or before/after an equals sign or ampersand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not add a hyphen to denote a line break or allow a hyphen that is part of the URL to appear at the line end. If necessary, break between words or syllables per word-division rules (7.36-47). Avoid forcing breaks in reflowable electronic publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notes format: basic structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A footnote or an endnote generally lists the author, title, and facts of publication, in that order; elements are separated by commas and the facts of publication are enclosed in parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors’ names are presented in standard order (first name first). Titles are capitalized headline-style unless in another language. Titles of larger works are italicized; titles of smaller works or unpublished works are roman and enclosed in quotation marks. Abbreviate editor/edited by, translator/translated by, volume, edition in notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bibliography entry format: basic structure
rubrics_metrics.description: In a bibliography entry the elements are separated by periods rather than commas; facts of publication are not enclosed in parentheses; the first-listed author's name is usually inverted for alphabetization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A bibliography entry starts with a capital letter unless the first word would normally be lowercased. Titles follow the same italicization/quotation rules as in notes. Abbreviations differ: noun forms (editor, translator, volume, edition) are abbreviated in bibliography, but verb forms (edited by, translated by) are spelled out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Page numbers and locators in notes vs bibliography
rubrics_metrics.description: In notes, give page numbers pertaining to the specific passage cited; in bibliographies, do not give page numbers for whole books but give the beginning and ending page numbers for journal articles or chapters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electronic sources may lack page numbers; in that case use chapter or paragraph numbers, section headings, or descriptive phrases following the work’s organization. For short searchable electronic works, locators may be unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shortened notes and use of bibliography
rubrics_metrics.description: If the bibliography includes all works cited in the notes, the notes need not duplicate full source information; in works with no bibliography or only a selected list, full details must be given in a note at first mention; subsequent citations can use a short form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice on constructing short forms is given in 14.29-36. In practice, using shortened forms in notes at first mention is acceptable when a full bibliography is present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author name formatting rules (notes vs bibliography; multiple authors)
rubrics_metrics.description: In notes, authors' names are presented in normal order; in bibliographies the first-listed author's name is inverted (last name first). For multiple authors, list all authors in the bibliography entry; in notes, cite only the first-listed author followed by et al. for four or more authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For two authors, invert only the first-listed name in the bibliography. For three authors list all in bibliography; notes cite as normal order (e.g., 'Alexander Berkman, Henry Bauer, and Carl Nold'). For four or more authors, cite first author et al. in notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor/translator credit differences in notes vs bibliography
rubrics_metrics.description: In a note, indicate editor/translator abbreviations (ed.; trans.); in the bibliography, spell out 'Edited by' or 'Translated by' and format accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Note: Gabriel Garcia Marquez, Love in the Time of Cholera, trans. Edith Grossman (London: Cape, 1988), 242–55. Bibliography: Garcia Marquez, Gabriel. Love in the Time of Cholera. Translated by Edith Grossman. London: Cape, 1988.

rubrics_metrics.name: Note reference number formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Note reference numbers in text are set as superior (superscript) numbers. In the notes themselves they are normally full size, not raised, and followed by a period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In manuscripts, superscript numbers in both places are acceptable as a typical default.
